name: Curiosity (MSL)
keyDiscovery: Curiosity confirmed that Gale Crater once held a freshwater lake with all six chemical elements essential for life (carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulphur).
missionLegacy: Curiosity proved Mars was once habitable for microbial life and pioneered the sky crane landing system now used by Perseverance — it continues to operate and climb Mount Sharp.
funFact: Curiosity carries a 1909 Lincoln penny on its calibration target — making it the only U.S. coin on Mars.
heritageNote: Curiosity remains operational at Gale Crater as of 2024, having driven over 30 km and climbed hundreds of metres up Mount Sharp; it is actively adding to its heritage every sol.

objects.name: Curiosity Rover
objects.description: Curiosity is a car-sized rover that landed on 6 August 2012 using an audacious sky crane manoeuvre. Weighing 899 kg, it is powered by a plutonium-238 radioisotope thermoelectric generator, so unlike Spirit and Opportunity, dust storms cannot end its mission. Curiosity carries 10 science instruments and has been climbing Mount Sharp since 2014.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Confirmed that Gale Crater once held a habitable freshwater lake environment with all six elements essential for life.
objects.legacy: Still operational and climbing Mount Sharp as of 2024, having driven over 30 km and drilled dozens of rock samples.
objects.firstPerson: Yo, make way for the nuclear beast! I am Curiosity! I am the size of an SUV, packing a nuclear reactor, a rock-vaporizing laser, and a full chemistry lab in my belly. For over twelve years I have been cruising Gale Crater, proving ancient Mars had freshwater lakes that could have supported microbial life. Nuclear-powered gigachad, still rolling strong!

objects.name: Sky Crane Descent Stage
objects.description: The sky crane hover stage lowered Curiosity on 7.6-metre nylon tethers, then flew away to crash-land 650 metres from the rover. This was the first use of the sky crane landing system. HiRISE images from orbit show the dark blast marks where its retrorockets hit the surface. The wreckage remains where it fell.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Demonstrated the first-ever sky crane landing, proving that heavy payloads can be precision-delivered to the Martian surface.
objects.legacy: The wreckage and blast marks are visible from orbit via HiRISE; the sky crane design was reused for Perseverance in 2021.
objects.firstPerson: Ayo, 7 Minutes of Terror champion! I am the Sky Crane. People thought rocket scientists were crazy: fire retro-rockets, hover 20 meters above Mars, lower a 1-ton rover on nylon cables, cut the cords, and fly away to crash in the distance! But it worked with 100% perfection. Coldest landing stunt ever performed in the galaxy!

objects.name: Drill Holes
objects.description: Curiosity has drilled dozens of holes into Martian bedrock, each about 1.6 cm wide and up to 6.5 cm deep. The powdered rock is delivered to the SAM and CheMin instruments inside the rover. Early drill samples at Yellowknife Bay revealed clay minerals and evidence of an ancient freshwater lake environment suitable for microbial life.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Delivered powdered rock to SAM and CheMin instruments, revealing clay minerals and organic molecules in Martian bedrock for the first time.
objects.legacy: Dozens of drill holes across Gale Crater mark Curiosity's path, each one a tiny window into Mars's ancient chemistry.
objects.firstPerson: Bro, tasting the fresh alien underground! We are the drill holes bored by Curiosity's robotic hammer-drill. We dug into ancient mudstones, sampled grey un-oxidized powder, and fed it to SAM and CheMin instruments, uncovering clay minerals and organic carbon molecules. Unlocking Martian history one hole at a time!

objects.name: Yellowknife Bay
objects.description: Yellowknife Bay was the first major science target. Curiosity found mudstone containing clay minerals, sulphate minerals, and the chemical elements needed for life: carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulphur. This discovery fulfilled the mission's primary goal: confirming that Mars once had environments habitable for microbes.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Contained mudstone with all six elements essential for life (C, H, N, O, P, S) plus clay minerals — fulfilling the mission's goal of confirming ancient habitability.
objects.legacy: Yellowknife Bay is where the habitability question was answered; Curiosity's drill holes there are among the most scientifically important marks on Mars.
objects.firstPerson: Hold up, proof of habitable Mars right here! I am Yellowknife Bay — an ancient lakebed where Curiosity drilled her very first rock. Lab tests confirmed my rocks were deposited in neutral, freshwater lakes with all the key elements for life: Carbon, Hydrogen, Oxygen, Nitrogen, Phosphorus, and Sulfur. Certified habitable zone!

objects.name: MAHLI Calibration Target
objects.description: Mounted on the rover's deck, the MAHLI calibration target includes a 1909 Lincoln penny (chosen for its fine detail), colour chips, a metric bar graphic, and a UV-fluorescent target. It is used to calibrate the Mars Hand Lens Imager. The penny belongs to principal investigator Ken Edgett — it is the only US coin on Mars.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Provides a known reference for colour, scale, and UV fluorescence so scientists can ensure MAHLI images are accurate across Mars's changing conditions.
objects.legacy: The 1909 Lincoln penny on Mars is a beloved cultural artefact — the only U.S. coin on another planet, still riding on Curiosity's deck.
objects.firstPerson: Ayo, check the drip! I carry a 1909 VDB Lincoln penny mounted on Curiosity's chassis! MAHLI camera zooms in on me to calibrate its lenses and colors before shooting microscopic rock photos. A genuine century-old copper coin chilling on Mars. Ultimate interplanetary swagger!

objects.name: Mount Sharp (Aeolis Mons)
objects.description: Rising 5.5 km above the crater floor, Mount Sharp is a layered mountain of sedimentary rock. Each layer records a chapter of Mars's environmental history. As Curiosity climbs, it reads that history: from clay-rich layers (wet era) through sulphate layers (drying era) to dry oxidised layers at the top. It is a geological time machine.
objects.scienceDiscovery: Its layered sedimentary rock records billions of years of Martian climate change — from a wet, habitable world to the cold, dry planet we see today.
objects.legacy: Mount Sharp is Curiosity's ongoing destination; the rover continues to climb and read Mars's environmental history layer by layer.
objects.firstPerson: Look up, space explorers! I am Mount Sharp — a colossal 5.5-kilometer mountain rising right from the center of Gale Crater! Taller than the Canadian Rockies! Curiosity has been climbing my sedimentary slopes layer by layer, reading millions of years of Martian climate history like an open book. King of the crater!
